name: Dice average
seoTitle: Dice average Calculator — Formula, Units & Example
seoDesc: Dice average: work out dice roll average from the dice roll standard deviation. A free statistics calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: The Dice average calculator returns dice roll average from the 2 fields on the form. No sign-up, no page reload, and the relationship behind it is printed below. That makes it useful for an assignment, a report or a data discussion where you need a defensible number. The unit chips sit next to the boxes, which is where most hand-calculation mistakes start.

sections.title: How does the Dice average calculator work?
sections.html:
The Dice average calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports dice roll average in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the dice type); then you type in the dice roll standard deviation.

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• Pick the option that matches your case — 6 options, such as tetrahedron (4 faces), cube (6 faces) and octahedron (8 faces). The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • A plain number with no unit attached.

One field on this form is a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the Dice average calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Dice roll average=die expected value × total number of dice
Total number of dice=3 × (dice roll standard deviation ^ 2) ÷ (die expected value × (die expected value − 1))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Dice type set to Tetrahedron (4 faces), Die expected value = 10 and Total number of dice = 10. Working through the relationship above gives Dice roll average = 100 and Dice roll standard deviation = 17.3205.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Dice roll average = 100 and Dice roll standard deviation = 17.3205 should be roughly the size you expected from Dice type set to Tetrahedron (4 faces) and Die expected value = 10.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Dice average calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Turning raw numbers into something you can quote
  • Checking a result a piece of software produced
  • Deciding how much confidence a sample really supports
  • Any time the same 1 figures keep coming back — the dice roll standard deviation — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.

sections.title: What are the limits worth knowing?
sections.html:
Every tool draws a boundary somewhere. For the Dice average calculator, these are the ones that matter:

  • The 1 drop-down on this page offers a fixed list of cases. A value that is not on the list cannot be entered, and the nearest option is not always a good substitute.
  • The calculator reports what the relationship implies; it does not judge whether the inputs themselves are sensible, so a figure that is out by a factor of ten will produce an answer that is out by the same factor.

faq.q: What does the Dice average calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns dice roll average, derived from the dice roll standard deviation. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Dice average calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the dice roll standard deviation, which is 2 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Dice roll average = 100. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Dice average calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
